parsed.summary: The Lean theorem states five facts about the Koebe map k(z)=z/(1−z)^2. It is schlicht on the unit disk. ∫_D |k'|^{-2} dA = ∞ and ∫_D |k'|^{2/3} dA = ∞. Its inverse g on the Koebe domain Ω = k(D) satisfies |g'|^4 ∉ L¹(Ω) and |g'|^{4/3} ∉ L¹(Ω). This is the classical sharpness example for the Brennan exponent range 4/3 < p < 4. The most important caveat: none of this appears in the supplied excerpt. That paper's Theorem 1.1, the uniform M_{-1}[f'](r) bound giving B_b(−1) < 1/4, is not formalized at all. The Lean content apparently belongs to the cited companion article on Brennan's conjecture, which is not in the excerpt.

f is univalent on D with f(0)=0 and f'(0)=1
glossary.note: deriv is the genuine derivative because f is holomorphic on the open disk containing 0.
The junk value at z=1 lies outside the open disk, so it is irrelevant.

glossary.plain: g = k^{-1} on Ω, chosen via invFunOn; arbitrary off Ω
glossary.note: On the open set Ω this agrees with the true inverse, so deriv there is the true g'. Values off Ω do not matter for IntegrableOn Ω.

glossary.standard_concept: area integral of a derivative power
glossary.note: A lintegral of ofReal, so a value of ⊤ means genuine divergence.

glossary.standard_concept: sharpness of Brennan's range at p=4 and p=4/3 via Koebe

lean_claims.plain: The Koebe function k is injective and holomorphic on D with k(0)=0 and k'(0)=1. Also ∫_D |k'|^{-2} dA = ∞ and ∫_D |k'|^{2/3} dA = ∞. Finally, with g = k^{-1} on Ω = k(D), the functions |g'|^4 and |g'|^{4/3} are not Lebesgue integrable on Ω.

paper_claims.plain: There exist 0 < ε < 1/4 and C < ∞ such that M_{-1}[f'](r) ≤ C(1−r)^{-1/4+ε} for all f ∈ S and all 1/2 ≤ r < 1. Consequently B_b(−1) < 1/4, and Kraetzer's conjecture fails at p=−1.
Distortion bounds (1−r)/(1+r)^3 ≤ |f'(z)| ≤ (1+r)/(1−r)^3, and the Koebe quarter theorem.
The normalized half-plane family K is compact, with the stated uniform bounds.

coverage.why: The Lean file says nothing about integral means M_{-1}, the spectrum B_b, or any uniform bound over S.
Not in excerpt. The Lean statement matches the classical Koebe sharpness example for Brennan's exponents 4/3 and 4, which this excerpt only references.

flags.explanation: The target theorem is about Koebe-map endpoint divergence for Brennan's conjecture, not the paper's main result, the uniform inverse-first-power bound and B_b(−1) < 1/4. The paper's headline claim is entirely unformalized. The formalized content is not stated in the excerpt.

¬IntegrableOn could in principle hold merely through failure of a.e.-strong measurability. Here deriv of any function ℂ→ℂ is measurable (measurable_deriv), so ¬IntegrableOn should mean genuine divergence. Only the endpoints are asserted; finiteness inside (4/3, 4) is not claimed.
flags.probe_idea: example : AEStronglyMeasurable (fun z => ‖deriv koebeInverse z‖ ^ (4:ℝ)) (volume.restrict koebeDomain) := by measurability / measurable_deriv

lint_verdicts.why: Differentiability on the open disk is required, so deriv f 0 is the true derivative.
The only zero denominator is at z=1, which lies outside the open unit disk.
A lintegral of a nonnegative function has no junk value; ⊤ means true divergence.
k is holomorphic on the open disk, so deriv agrees with k' there.
An ℝ≥0∞ value is appropriate for expressing divergence.
ofReal of a nonnegative real is exact; 0^{-2} occurs only at z=−1, which is on the boundary and measure zero.
(2/3 : ℝ) is real division, not ℕ division.
invFunOn yields the true inverse on the open set Ω, so deriv is local and correct there.
